name: Merry Widow corset

lead: The Merry Widow is a long-line bra-and-corset hybrid: a strapless piece with cups, boning and a nipped waist that extends over the midsection, often with loops for suspenders. Worn under clothing, it gives an hourglass shape by cinching the waist and supporting the bust.

The style took its name from a Warner's line launched in 1952 and remained popular through the 1950s. The effect is temporary and works through compression and structure, and it is used under fitted dresses and costume or vintage-style outfits.

paras: It is worn as foundation underneath dresses or other fitted clothes, fastened with hooks and eyes at the back, sometimes with suspenders attached to hold stockings. Vintage-style wearers pair it with strapless or off-the-shoulder garments.

As with other boned, cinching garments, a tight fit can limit breathing and movement and cause discomfort over long wear; sizing and fit determine comfort. The shaping disappears when the garment is removed.

angle.text: The Merry Widow directly shapes the torso while worn: boning and waist reinforcement compress the waist and the cups support and lift the bust, giving an hourglass outline under strapless and fitted clothing.

lead: A Merry Widow is a longline corselet or 'cinch-bra': a strapless foundation garment combining underwired cups with boning and a snug waist section that reaches below the bust over the midriff, usually closed with hook-and-eye tape at the back and often fitted with detachable suspenders [1]. It is worn to create a fashionable hourglass outline, smoothing the waist and lifting the bust under fitted clothing [1][2].

Warner's, the American corset maker founded in 1874, launched its first Merry Widow line in 1952; the name refers to Lana Turner's film The Merry Widow of that year, although museum sources say the garments did not appear in it [1][2]. Advertising promised a smaller waist, and lightweight nylon tulle and stretch panels made it lighter than older cotton-coutil corsetry [1][2]. The style was produced into the 1960s [2].

paras: A museum example from Warner's is described as a longline cinch-bra of sheer nylon tulle with stretch panels, a wide satin ribbon at the waist, picot elastic edging and a hook-and-eye back closure. The cups use three pattern pieces with underwires encased in satin tape, and 5 mm spiral steel boning runs over the underwire to the bust seam [1]. Loops carry detachable suspenders [1].

Warner Brothers Corset Manufacturers was founded in 1874 by Dr Lucien Warner and his brother, bought Mary Phelps Jacob's brassiere patent in 1915, introduced lettered cup sizing in the 1930s, and launched the Merry Widow line in 1952 [1]. The Museum at FIT says the line was inspired by the 1952 film and promoted a waist reduction of up to three inches, and it notes that another source gives 1953 [2]. The garment suited the strapless and off-the-shoulder dresses of the era after Dior's 1947 New Look made a defined waist fashionable, a style for which waist cinchers were also worn [3]. Lightweight synthetics suited the 1950s travel boom [1].
